name: Anterior open bite correction

card.summary: Orthodontic, surgical or myofunctional treatment that closes the gap between the front teeth, improving the bite, smile and lower-face proportions.
card.note: Relapse is common after treatment; surgery carries the usual operative risks and requires specialist assessment.

quick.overview:
An anterior open bite is a bite in which the upper and lower front teeth do not overlap or touch when the back teeth close. Correcting it can improve how the smile and lower third of the face look, and it also improves biting function and sometimes speech.

Treatment depends on the cause and the age of the patient. Habit correction and myofunctional therapy are used in children; braces, elastics, clear aligners and mini-screws are used in adults with dental open bites; and jaw surgery is used for skeletal cases. Systematic reviews exist on stability, and relapse is a recognised issue.
quick.how: An orthodontist or oral surgeon diagnoses whether the open bite is dental, skeletal or functional. In growing children, habits such as thumb sucking are addressed and tongue-posture exercises or appliances may be used. In adults, options include fixed braces with mini-screw anchorage to intrude back teeth, clear aligners, and orthognathic surgery. Looksmaxxing forums discuss myofunctional work as a non-surgical route.
quick.risks: Relapse is the main issue; a 2011 meta-analysis put stability around 75 percent after non-surgical and 82 percent after surgical correction. Molar intrusion carries a risk of root resorption, and jaw surgery carries risks including joint changes. Treatment planning belongs with a qualified orthodontist or surgeon.

lead: Anterior open bite (AOB) is a malocclusion in which the front teeth fail to meet vertically while the back teeth close [1][2]. Reviews describe it as both an aesthetic and a functional handicap, with the lower third of the face appearing disproportionately large in skeletal cases [1].

People seek correction to improve how the smile, lips and lower face look and to restore biting with the front teeth. Approaches range from habit control and myofunctional therapy in children to orthodontic appliances, skeletal anchorage and orthognathic surgery in adults [1][3][4].

Research on open bite treatment is extensive, including systematic reviews, meta-analyses and randomized trials. The literature repeatedly identifies long-term stability as the central challenge [5][6].

chain: Identify cause: habit, tongue posture, dental or skeletal
Close the gap with myofunctional work, orthodontics or surgery
Front teeth meet; smile and lower-face proportions improve
angle.text: Closing the open bite brings the front teeth into contact, which changes the smile line and, in skeletal cases, can reduce lower facial height. Many people also report better function when biting and speaking.

paras: Open bite is a malocclusion in which the front teeth do not touch or overlap when the jaws close. Wikipedia reports prevalence estimates of 1.5 to 11 percent depending on definition, falling with age [7]. Clinicians classify AOB as dental, skeletal or functional [8]. Skeletal cases are associated with a long lower face, and sometimes a gummy smile [7].

Oral habits such as thumb sucking, tongue thrusting and mouth breathing are strongly associated with anterior open bite in children [9][10]. Other contributors include enlarged tongue or tonsils and a vertical growth pattern [7].

Early treatment is described as controversial, and a systematic review of treatments in the mixed dentition assessed effectiveness and stability of early correction [3]. A review of atypical swallowing compared orthodontic treatment, speech therapy and the two combined [4]. Randomized trials have examined orofacial myofunctional therapy and tongue behaviour in children with open bite [11][12].

Non-surgical options include extrusion arches and the Multiloop Edgewise Archwire technique, and mini-screws are used for anchorage and vertical control [8]. Clear aligners have been studied for molar intrusion in adults with open bite [13][14]. Skeletal cases have traditionally required surgery [8]; a review traces options from classical orthodontics to combined orthodontic-surgical approaches with anchorage systems [1].

A meta-analysis of molar intrusion with skeletal anchorage found a mean overbite relapse of about 1.2 mm over an average follow-up of 2.5 years [6]. A randomized trial of 40 adults compared clear aligners with fixed appliances plus miniscrews for molar intrusion, measuring root resorption and bite force [13]. A 2023 study examined the predictability of open bite treatment with Invisalign [14]. Randomized trials have examined myofunctional therapy and tongue pressure as predictors of correction [11][12], and a two-year follow-up trial assessed stability of early treatment [15]. An older meta-analysis assessed stability of treatment for AOB [16].

Relapse is common: Wikipedia cites a 2011 meta-analysis reporting about 82 percent stability after surgical and about 75 percent after non-surgical correction [7][16]. Studies of Le Fort I and bimaxillary osteotomies in open bite patients have described condylar remodelling and resorption [17]. Root resorption was a measured outcome in molar-intrusion trials [13].
